d1.overview: Domain I establishes the conceptual bedrock: what AI is, the forms it takes, the risks and harms it creates, why those risks demand governance, and how an organization organizes people, policies and processes to respond. The BOK is explicit that the domain covers "best practices regardless of industry, sector or size", so nothing here is sector-specific. It runs from technology literacy (model types, learning paradigms) through organizational readiness (roles, collaboration, training) to policy (lifecycle oversight, legacy policy updates, third-party risk).
d1.deep_dive:
Domain I carries **16 to 20 of the 100 scored items**, split across three competencies. It is the smallest domain by question count and the one with the most downstream reach: the vocabulary and principle set it installs are the raw material every later domain reasons with.

| Competency | What it covers | Questions |
|---|---|---|
| **I.A** Understand what AI is and why it needs governance | Definitions and types of AI; risks and harms; the characteristics that demand governance; responsible AI principles | 4 to 6 |
| **I.B** Establish and communicate organizational expectations | Roles and responsibilities; cross-functional collaboration; training and awareness; tailoring by context; developers, providers, deployers and users | 5 to 7 |
| **I.C** Establish policies and procedures across the life cycle | Oversight and accountability at every stage; updating existing privacy, security, data-governance and IP policies; third-party risk | 6 to 8 |

### How the BOK frames it

The BOK describes Domain I as "what AI governance is, including the common principles and pillars to build an AI governance program", and repeats that this holds "regardless of industry, sector or size." That framing is itself testable. An answer that assumes a bank, a hospital or a large enterprise is usually the wrong one, because Domain I is where the generic, transferable practice lives; sector specifics belong to Domain II's sectoral laws and to the lifecycle domains.

The BOK also states that exam items sit mostly at the **remember/understand** and **apply/analyze** levels of Bloom's taxonomy. Domain I is where the remember/understand share is highest, which is why definitional precision pays here more than anywhere else.

### What changed in BOK v2.1

Three v2.1 edits land inside Domain I:

- **I.B now lists providers** alongside developers, deployers and users. The added role matters because a provider can be a small team that fine-tunes someone else's base model, so the BOK wants you to see the value chain rather than only the internal cast.
- **I.C's policy-review item now names data governance and intellectual property** explicitly, alongside the data privacy and security policies that v2.0.1 already listed.
- **I.C's third-party item now covers policies, assessments and contracts**, and adds **acceptable use** to the areas (procurement, supply chain, human resources) it names.

### How to hold the domain

Treat Domain I as two halves. The first (I.A) is descriptive: classify a system, name what can go wrong, and name the characteristic that makes the failure mode possible. The second (I.B and I.C) is organizational: say who is accountable, what has to be written down, and which legacy policy an AI use case has just broken. Nearly every Domain I item is one of those two moves.
d1.exam:
Worth roughly 16 to 20 questions, the smallest of the four domains, and the one where definitional precision is worth the most points. Expect narrow vs. general AI, supervised vs. unsupervised vs. reinforcement learning, and functionality ladders, then scenario items about assigning governance roles, updating pre-AI policies, and managing third-party AI risk.

Two patterns recur. First, a question gives you a system and asks you to classify it or name the harm it presents; the answer follows from vocabulary you either have cold or don't. Second, a question describes an organization adopting AI and asks what the governance professional should do first or next. Those answers reward the same instincts that pay across the whole exam: risk-based proportionality, documented decisions, and multidisciplinary involvement.

Because I.C carries the most items (6 to 8), do not under-weight policy work. The most common trap is treating Domain I as pure theory and spending all your revision time on the technical taxonomy.

The BOK's four I.A indicators are definitions and types, risks and harms, governance-demanding characteristics, and responsible AI principles
I.A's governance-demanding characteristics: complexity, opacity, autonomy, speed and scale, potential for harm or misuse, data dependency, probabilistic versus deterministic outputs

ch1.overview: This knowledge area defines the technology being governed and makes the case for governing it. It walks the AI taxonomies (capability, functionality, technique, learning paradigm), catalogs the risks and harms AI creates for individuals, groups, organizations and society, identifies the characteristics that make AI uniquely hard to govern, and lands on the responsible AI principles that answer those characteristics. Four performance indicators, four sections, one vocabulary.
ch1.deep_dive:
I.A is the domain's vocabulary engine. Each of its four performance indicators maps onto one section of the knowledge area, and the exam tests them separately.

### 1. Definitions and types of AI

Three overlapping taxonomies get used, and questions mix them freely:

| Taxonomy | Levels | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Capability or scope** | Narrow (weak) AI to artificial general intelligence to artificial superintelligence | Only narrow AI exists today, whatever a product page claims |
| **Functionality** | Reactive machines, limited memory, theory of mind, self-aware | The last two are conceptual only |
| **Learning paradigm** | Supervised, unsupervised, semi-supervised, reinforcement, self-supervised | This is how practitioners actually describe a system |

The legally operative definition is not in any of those tables. Both the OECD's 2023 revision and Article 3 of the EU AI Act define an AI system functionally: a machine-based system that, for explicit or implicit objectives, **infers** from the input it receives how to generate outputs such as predictions, content, recommendations or decisions that can influence physical or virtual environments. "Infers" is the load-bearing word, because it is what separates AI from ordinary rule-following software. ISO/IEC 22989 supplies the parallel formal vocabulary (AI system, AI model, AI component, and the role terms provider, producer, customer, user and AI subject) that the management-system standards lean on.

### 2. Risks and harms

The BOK names three examples for this indicator: **misalignment with objectives**, **ethics and bias risk**, and **complexity and scalability**. Around them sits the standard four-way breakdown by who is harmed:

| Who is harmed | Representative harms |
|---|---|
| **Individuals** | Privacy invasion, discriminatory decisions in employment or credit, safety failures, manipulation, loss of autonomy |
| **Groups** | Bias amplification against protected classes, feedback loops that compound disadvantage, erosion of social cohesion |
| **Organizations** | Regulatory penalties, litigation, reputational damage, IP contamination, security exposure, operational failure |
| **Society** | Misinformation and deepfakes, displacement of work, concentration of power, environmental cost |

Generative systems add their own signature failures: confabulation (the formal term for hallucination), synthetic media abuse at scale, and the privacy exposure that comes from training on unfiltered web data.

### 3. Characteristics that demand governance

The BOK's list is: **complexity, opacity, autonomy, speed and scale, potential for harm or misuse, data dependency, and probabilistic versus deterministic outputs.** The useful mental move is to pair each characteristic with the control it motivates, because exam items usually ask why a control exists:

| Characteristic | Why it defeats ordinary software governance | Control it motivates |
|---|---|---|
| Complexity | Many interacting components and emergent behaviour resist review and root-cause analysis | Layered testing, documentation, auditability |
| Opacity | Even builders cannot fully explain a deep model's output | Explainability work, model cards, disclosure duties |
| Autonomy | Decisions execute without a human between inference and effect | Human oversight design, action limits, kill switches |
| Speed and scale | One flaw replicates across millions of decisions before anyone notices | Pre-deployment testing, continuous monitoring, rollback |
| Potential for harm or misuse | Surveillance, manipulation, weaponisation, fraud | Impact assessment, ethics review, security controls |
| Data dependency | Quality, provenance and bias of training data drive outcomes | Data governance, lineage, bias testing |
| Probabilistic outputs | The system is statistically confident, not correct | Thresholds, confidence handling, monitoring, user training |

### 4. Responsible AI principles

The BOK lists **fairness, safety and reliability, privacy and security, transparency and explainability, accountability, and human-centricity.** These are the same substance as the OECD's five principles and NIST's seven trustworthiness characteristics, relabelled; the exam expects you to recognise the concept under whichever label the stem uses.

One distinction is worth committing to memory because it is a reliable distractor: **transparency** is about the organization disclosing that AI is in use and how, while **explainability** is about whether a specific output can be understood by the person affected by it. **Interpretability** sits underneath both, as the property of a model whose internal behaviour can be inspected at all.
ch1.exam:
The exam's vocabulary heartland, and the place where definitional questions cluster. Be able to classify an example system instantly: a recommender is narrow AI, a system that perceives its environment and acts on it is an agent, a model trained on labelled pairs is supervised learning, a rule-based medical advisor is an expert system. Then be able to match a harm or a characteristic to the principle or control that answers it.

Two traps repeat. First, options that treat a current product as general AI or as self-aware are wrong by definition; only narrow AI exists. Second, transparency, explainability and interpretability are routinely offered as interchangeable answers, and only one of them fits the stem. Read which party the question is asking about: the organization disclosing, or the affected individual understanding a decision.

The BOK's harm examples are misalignment with objectives, ethics and bias risk, and complexity and scalability

ch2.overview: This knowledge area is about the humans: which roles carry AI governance (from board and C-suite through data scientists and privacy professionals), how cross-functional collaboration is structured, what training and awareness programs must cover, how governance is tailored to organizational context, and the developer / provider / deployer / user distinction that allocates responsibility along the AI value chain. Its underlying claim is that governance is a shared responsibility, not a department.
ch2.deep_dive:
I.B is the organizational half of Domain I, and the BOK gives it five performance indicators covering roles, collaboration, training, context and value-chain position.

### Roles and responsibilities

The BOK asks you to "define roles and responsibilities for AI governance stakeholders" without prescribing an org chart, which is the point: governance is a shared responsibility spanning disciplines, and should not be centralized in a single team. In practice an effective program has three layers.

| Layer | Who | What they own |
|---|---|---|
| **Direction** | Board, CEO, CRO, CISO, CDAO, CPO, CCO | Risk appetite, funding, tone, accountability for outcomes |
| **Steering** | A cross-functional AI governance board or council | Framework ownership, high-risk use-case review, escalation as final reviewer, reporting upward |
| **Operating** | Legal, privacy, security, data science, AI ops, ethics, compliance, product owners, frontline users | Building, assessing, monitoring, documenting, reporting anomalies |

The BOK's framing of governance as part of overall corporate **due care** is worth internalizing: organizations that face legal trouble over an AI system are judged worse when no governance program existed at all.

### Cross-functional collaboration

The BOK states the purpose of collaboration directly: efficacy and **diversity of expertise and perspective**. A single function rarely has both business relevance and technical depth, so centralizing governance produces either an academic exercise or a rubber stamp. The practical instruments are a standing cross-functional working group, use-case reviews triggered by defined risk conditions (automated decisions affecting rights, sensitive or biometric data, employment or lending or medical impact, low explainability, rising regulatory scrutiny), and shared artifacts such as model cards, risk assessment forms and impact assessments.

### Training and awareness

The BOK requires a program delivered "to all stakeholders on AI terminology, strategy and governance." Two design rules follow from that wording. First, awareness for everyone, depth by role: executives need risk literacy and regulatory exposure, developers need governance by design and bias testing, users need to understand capabilities, limits and appropriate reliance. Second, the program has to be maintained, because a curriculum written before the current obligations existed does not satisfy them. Since 2 February 2025 the EU AI Act has made AI literacy an explicit expectation for provider and deployer staff, which turns training from a culture initiative into a compliance item.

### Tailoring to organizational context

The BOK asks you to differentiate governance by **company size, maturity, industry, products and services, objectives and risk tolerance.** That is a proportionality instruction: a startup governs with a principles charter, a named champion and lightweight checklists, while a large enterprise builds a federated structure wired into enterprise risk management, with tooling and automation. Maturity models (COBIT-style, from nonexistent through initial, repeatable, defined, managed, optimized) give you the vocabulary for the second axis. The exam-relevant nuance: high maturity is not automatically the goal, and low risk tolerance should never mean no governance, only more conservative gates.

### Developers, providers, deployers and users

BOK v2.1 adds **providers** to the roles this indicator names. The BOK also states, in its introduction, that "developer" and "deployer" are used as **task labels, not legal categories**, which matters because the EU AI Act uses a partly different cast (provider, deployer, importer, distributor) with obligations attached. Keep the two vocabularies separate in your head: the BOK's developer builds and trains, the deployer operationalizes and monitors, the user operates within intended bounds, and the provider is the entity that places the system on the market under its own name.
ch2.exam:
Scenario questions ask who should be involved, who is accountable, or what a committee's composition should achieve. The dominant pattern is that an answer concentrating AI governance in one function (legal, IT, data science) is engineered to be wrong; the correct answer is multidisciplinary, and usually names the affected business function too.

The developer / provider / deployer / user split matters here and returns in the EU AI Act's provider / deployer / importer / distributor roles. A reliable trap: an entity that rebrands or substantially modifies a high-risk system becomes the provider and inherits provider duties, so read the stem for who is acting under whose name. Also expect a training question where the wrong answers are one-size-fits-all; role-tailored awareness plus depth where it counts is the answer the BOK is looking for.

ch3.overview: This knowledge area confronts the fact that most organizations' policies predate AI. It covers oversight of autonomous decision-making, the specific ways AI breaks existing privacy, security, data-governance and intellectual-property policy assumptions (inference, model retention, re-identification, new attack surfaces), and the third-party risk problem: pretrained models, APIs and data suppliers that traditional vendor management was never built to probe. It carries the largest share of Domain I items.
ch3.deep_dive:
I.C is the largest competency in Domain I at 6 to 8 questions, and it is the most practical. The BOK assumes **IT governance already exists**: AI governance activities sit on top of it, not in place of it. From there the competency has three indicators.

### 1. Oversight and accountability across every lifecycle stage

The BOK names nine stages that policies must reach: **use case assessment, risk management, ethics by design, data acquisition and use, model and system development, training and testing, deployment and monitoring, documentation and reporting, and incident management.** The governance move is not to write nine documents; it is to place a decision point and an owner at each stage, so that nothing consequential happens without a named accountable human.

In practice that means policies that are risk-calibrated (stricter for high-stakes uses), versioned and auditable, embedded in the technical workflow rather than parallel to it, and operationalized through gates, templates, checklists and records. Three artifacts do most of the work:

- **A use-case assessment gate** before any build, asking whether AI is the right tool, what harm is possible, whether sufficient quality data exists, and whether a simpler rule-based solution would do.
- **A go/no-go decision point** at the end of testing, where management reviews results and records the decision.
- **An AI-specific incident playbook**, tested and rehearsed, because detection capability has to exist before you can declare an incident.

### 2. Updating existing policies for AI

The BOK names four policy families to evaluate and update: **data privacy, security, data governance and intellectual property** (v2.1 added the last two explicitly). Each breaks in a characteristic way:

| Legacy policy | How AI breaks it | What the update has to say |
|---|---|---|
| **Data privacy** | Data is repurposed for training, retained inside model weights, and sensitive traits are inferred from ordinary inputs | Purpose-limitation analysis for secondary use, retention rules covering derived data and models, a position on deletion requests against trained models |
| **Security** | New attack surface: model inversion, membership inference, data poisoning, prompt injection, model theft | AI in threat modelling, monitoring for AI-specific telemetry, pipeline and model-registry controls |
| **Data governance** | Provenance and quality were never recorded because no model depended on them | Lineage and provenance requirements, quality dimensions, dataset ownership, representativeness checks |
| **Intellectual property** | Training on third-party works, unclear output ownership, leaked trade secrets into prompts | Training-data rights review, machine-readable opt-out handling, output-ownership position, acceptable-use rules for external tools |

A prerequisite the BOK states plainly: you need a **data classification policy and a data inventory** first. Without them, managing and monitoring AI training data is severely disadvantaged, and no amount of AI-specific policy will compensate.

### 3. Third-party risk

The BOK names four areas: **procurement, supply chain, human resources and acceptable use** (the last added in v2.1), and covers **policies, assessments and contracts**. The core observation is that traditional third-party risk management checks solvency, insurance and certification, while AI risk arrives as opaque training data, sub-tier labelling suppliers, silently changing model versions and unclear liability for harmful output.

The governance answer has four parts: flag AI at procurement intake so the deal gets supplemental review; run AI-specific due diligence (training-data origin and rights, fairness and robustness evidence, explainability support, model-change practices); write the contract terms that make the risk manageable (data-use limits, performance and fairness warranties, model-change and incident notification, audit rights, termination and portability); and monitor continuously, because a vendor model update can change behaviour mid-contract. An **AI system bill of materials** listing upstream inputs is the emerging instrument for the sub-tier problem.

The non-negotiable: accountability is not delegable. Outsourcing the AI does not outsource the regulatory or ethical responsibility.
ch3.exam:
Expect scenarios about a company adopting AI under legacy policies: what gap exists, what to update first, what contract terms to demand from an AI vendor. The strongest answers name a concrete broken assumption (retention schedules that never contemplated model weights, incident response that has no playbook for prompt injection, a data inventory that does not exist) rather than saying "update the policies."

Two other reliable angles. First, human oversight levels: human-in-the-loop versus human-on-the-loop, and the requirement that oversight be meaningful rather than a rubber stamp. Second, sequencing: use-case assessment and impact assessment come before build, the go/no-go decision comes at the end of testing, and policies must be calibrated to risk rather than uniform. If an option proposes treating a high-stakes system and an internal productivity tool identically, it is wrong.

t_ai_types.overview: The classification system for everything the exam calls "AI": capability levels (narrow AI that exists, AGI and ASI that do not yet), functionality levels (reactive machines through the theoretical self-aware systems), the machine-learning family tree (supervised, unsupervised, semi-supervised, reinforcement, self-supervised), and the modern generative stack (neural networks, deep learning, transformers, large language models, foundation models).
t_ai_types.deep_dive:
Four taxonomies cover almost every classification question, and they answer different questions.

### By capability

| Level | Meaning | Exists today? |
|---|---|---|
| **Narrow (weak) AI** | Performs a specific task or narrow task family | Yes. Every deployed system, however impressive |
| **General AI (AGI)** | Human-level competence across essentially all cognitive domains | No |
| **Superintelligence (ASI)** | Surpasses the best human performance in essentially every domain | No |

The trap here is breadth. A large language model answering questions about law, medicine and poetry is still narrow AI, because generality is about transfer across unrelated domains the way a person does it, not about the size of the training set.

### By functionality

Reactive machines respond to input with no memory of it (the chess engine that evaluates only the current position). Limited memory systems retain recent context to inform the next decision (autonomous vehicles, and in practice most modern systems). Theory of mind and self-aware AI are conceptual categories, not deployed technology.

### By learning paradigm

| Paradigm | Data | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| **Supervised** | Labelled input-output pairs | Learns the mapping from labels |
| **Unsupervised** | Unlabelled data | Finds structure, clusters, anomalies |
| **Semi-supervised** | A little labelled plus a lot unlabelled | Uses structure to extend scarce labels |
| **Reinforcement** | A reward signal from interaction | Learns a policy that maximises reward |
| **Self-supervised** | Raw data, with the labels derived from the data itself | The paradigm behind modern language models |

### The generative stack

Deep learning stacks neural network layers; transformers made attention practical at scale and enabled large language models; foundation models are broad pretrained models adapted to downstream tasks by fine-tuning or prompting. Two governance-relevant properties come out of that lineage. Scale buys capability, sometimes abruptly: the literature on emergent abilities documents behaviours that appear only past a size threshold, which is why a model's capabilities cannot always be enumerated in advance. And pretrained models carry their training data's properties into every downstream use, including its biases.

### Agents

An AI agent perceives its environment and takes action toward goals, rather than only returning a prediction when asked. Perception plus action is the tell. Agentic architectures matter to governance because they move AI from advising a human to acting on the world, which is where the oversight and action-limit questions begin.
t_ai_types.exam:
Pure classification: given an example, name the type. A chess engine is a reactive machine; an autonomous vehicle uses limited memory; a chat assistant is narrow AI despite its breadth; a spam filter trained on labelled mail is supervised learning; a recommender finding clusters in unlabelled behaviour is unsupervised; a robot learning to navigate by reward is reinforcement learning. Get these to reflex speed, because they are free points and they underpin harder scenario items later.

The recurring trap is breadth versus generality, and the second is a system that acts. If a stem says the system takes actions in an environment, the answer is agent, not model.

t_ai_risks.overview: The harm catalog that motivates all of AI governance, organized by who gets hurt: individuals (privacy invasion, discriminatory decisions, safety), groups (bias amplification against protected classes), organizations (liability, reputational damage, IP leakage), and society (misinformation and deepfakes, displacement of work, eroded autonomy, environmental cost). The BOK names misalignment with objectives, ethics and bias risk, and complexity and scalability as its three examples.
t_ai_risks.deep_dive:
### The four-way sort

| Who is harmed | Representative harms |
|---|---|
| **Individuals** | Privacy violation, discriminatory decisions in hiring or credit, physical safety failure, manipulation, loss of autonomy |
| **Groups** | Systematic bias against protected classes, amplification through feedback loops, erosion of shared factual ground |
| **Organizations** | Regulatory penalty, litigation, reputational damage, IP contamination, security exposure, operational disruption |
| **Society** | Misinformation and deepfakes, displacement of work, concentration of capability, environmental cost of training and inference |

The BOK's own three examples cut across the sort. **Misalignment with objectives** is the case where the system optimises the metric it was given rather than the outcome anyone wanted. **Ethics and bias risk** is unfair or harmful treatment that the data or the objective encoded. **Complexity and scalability** is the multiplier: a flaw in a manual process harms the people it touches, while the same flaw in a deployed model harms everyone it scores before anyone notices.

### Generative-specific failures

NIST's Generative AI Profile names twelve risks unique to or amplified by generative AI. The exam-relevant ones are **confabulation** (the formal term for hallucination: confidently stated, plausible, false output, which is a property of the paradigm rather than an occasional bug), **harmful bias and homogenization**, **information integrity** (the deepfake and disinformation problem), **data privacy**, **information security**, **intellectual property**, and **value-chain and component integration** risk, which is the risk you inherit from the models and data you did not build.

### Why the sort matters operationally

The category determines who owns the response. An individual harm usually triggers a rights or recourse process; a group harm triggers fairness testing and remediation; an organizational harm runs through the risk register and the board; a societal harm may have no internal owner at all, which is exactly why impact assessments exist. A harm that is not assigned to a category tends not to get a control.
t_ai_risks.exam:
Questions ask you to identify the harm category in a scenario, or to pick the governance response proportionate to it. Distinguish individual from group from societal harm, and remember that a single incident usually lands in several categories at once: an employment screening model that penalises a protected class harms the applicants, the class, the employer and the labour market.

Hallucination or confabulation is the signature generative risk and a frequent correct answer. An option asserting that a well-tested model cannot be confidently wrong is wrong by construction.

t_ai_char.overview: Why AI cannot be governed like ordinary software: models are opaque (even builders cannot fully explain outputs), autonomous (acting without per-decision human review), probabilistic (confidently wrong), fast and scalable (one flaw replicated across millions of decisions), emergent (capabilities appearing unplanned), and data-hungry (creating pressure that breaks privacy assumptions). The BOK names seven: complexity, opacity, autonomy, speed and scale, potential for harm or misuse, data dependency, and probabilistic versus deterministic outputs.
t_ai_char.deep_dive:
The exam almost always asks this indicator indirectly: "which characteristic of AI makes this control necessary?" So learn each characteristic as a pair with the control it justifies.

| Characteristic | What it defeats | Control it justifies |
|---|---|---|
| **Complexity** | Human intuition and simple review; many interacting parts and emergent behaviour | Layered testing, documentation, auditability, decomposition into components |
| **Opacity** | The ability to explain a specific decision to the person affected | Explainability techniques, model cards, disclosure duties, contestability |
| **Autonomy** | The assumption that a human is in the decision loop | Human oversight design, action limits, interruption and override, kill switches |
| **Speed and scale** | The assumption that errors are caught locally and slowly | Pre-deployment testing, continuous monitoring, defined rollback criteria |
| **Potential for harm or misuse** | The assumption that capability is used as intended | Impact assessment, ethics review, security controls, red teaming |
| **Data dependency** | The assumption that behaviour is specified in code | Data governance, lineage and provenance, representativeness and bias testing |
| **Probabilistic outputs** | Binary notions of correct and incorrect | Confidence thresholds, abstention, monitoring, user training against over-trust |

### The two that surprise people

**Probabilistic versus deterministic output** is easy to gloss over and heavily tested. Traditional software is deterministic: the same input yields the same output, and a defect is a deviation from specification. A model produces a statistical estimate, so the same input may yield different outputs, and being wrong is a property of the paradigm rather than a bug. That is why "the model is accurate 97% of the time" is a governance statement about residual risk, not a clean bill of health.

**Data dependency** is what makes AI governance inseparable from data governance. The system's behaviour is learned from data whose provenance, representativeness and quality determine the outcome, which is why lineage, provenance and bias testing appear in every framework and, for high-risk systems, in law.

### Emergence is the odd one out

The BOK's list is a set of characteristics, not a taxonomy, so it is worth adding the one that sits behind several of them: **emergence**. Capabilities and behaviours can appear after deployment through scale, fine-tuning, data drift or interaction with other systems. Emergence is the reason point-in-time approval is insufficient and why monitoring and re-assessment are continuous rather than one-off.
t_ai_char.exam:
Expect stems of the form "which characteristic of AI makes X necessary." Opacity motivates explainability requirements; autonomy motivates human oversight; speed and scale motivate pre-deployment testing and rollback planning; probabilistic output motivates confidence handling, monitoring and user training; data dependency motivates lineage and bias testing.

The most reliable distractor is determinism. An option that assumes a model behaves like conventional software (same input, same output, defects trace to code) contradicts the probabilistic-output characteristic, so it is wrong whenever the stem involves a learned model.

t_rai.overview: The principle set that answers AI's risk profile. The BOK's list is fairness, safety and reliability, privacy and security, transparency and explainability, accountability, and human-centricity. These recur in every major framework (the OECD's five principles, NIST's seven trustworthiness characteristics, the EU AI Act's requirements) with different labels but the same substance, which is why the exam can test them under any framework's name.
t_rai.deep_dive:
### The BOK's six, and what each demands

| Principle | What it requires | How it is operationalized |
|---|---|---|
| **Fairness** | Equitable treatment and outcomes across groups | Bias testing across subgroups, fairness metrics chosen for context, mitigation, documentation of trade-offs |
| **Safety and reliability** | Intended function under expected and unexpected conditions | Rigorous testing, edge-case and adversarial testing, fail-safes, interruptability, continuous monitoring |
| **Privacy and security** | Personal data protected, systems resilient to attack | Minimization, de-identification, access control, AI-specific threat modelling, pipeline security |
| **Transparency and explainability** | People know AI is in use and can understand outcomes affecting them | Disclosure, instructions for use, explanations of decisions, documentation, contestability |
| **Accountability** | Identified humans answer for outcomes | Named owners, RACI, escalation paths, audit rights, records |
| **Human-centricity** | AI augments human agency rather than overriding it | Human oversight for consequential decisions, impact assessment, design that preserves choice |

### Where the labels come from

The same substance appears under three vocabularies, and the exam expects you to translate:

- **OECD (2019, revised 2024)**: inclusive growth and well-being; human rights, rule of law and democratic values (including fairness and privacy); transparency and explainability; robustness, security and safety; accountability.
- **NIST AI RMF**: valid and reliable; safe; secure and resilient; accountable and transparent; explainable and interpretable; privacy-enhanced; fair with harmful bias managed.
- **EU AI Act**: risk management, data governance, technical documentation, record-keeping, transparency and instructions for use, human oversight, accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity for high-risk systems, plus the Article 50 transparency duties.

### The distinctions worth memorizing

**Transparency versus explainability.** Transparency is about the organization: that AI is in use, what it does, what its limits are. Explainability is about a specific output: whether the person affected can understand why it came out that way. Interpretability is the underlying model property that makes explanation possible at all.

**Accountability versus responsibility.** Responsibility is who does the work; accountability is who answers for the outcome. Accountability cannot be delegated to a model or a vendor, which is the failure mode every accountability framework exists to prevent.

**Fairness is plural.** Several fairness metrics cannot hold simultaneously except in degenerate cases, so "make it fair" is not a specification. The governance answer is to choose metrics appropriate to the context, document the trade-off, and test across subgroups.

### Principles are the tiebreaker

When two exam answers both look defensible, the one that honours more of these principles, and does so with documentation and proportionality, is almost always the intended answer.
t_rai.exam:
Expect matching questions (principle to definition, or principle to the framework that names it) and scenarios asking which principle a control serves. Transparency versus explainability is the classic trap pair, and so is accountability versus responsibility.

A second pattern: a scenario describes a control (a bias audit, an oversight checkpoint, a disclosure notice, a model card) and asks which principle it advances. Bias audit is fairness; oversight checkpoint is human-centricity or accountability depending on whether the question is about the human or the owner; disclosure is transparency; a model card is usually transparency and explainability together. Where an option bundles the principles into a single-function answer ("assign it to legal"), it is wrong.
key_points: The BOK's six principles: fairness, safety and reliability, privacy and security, transparency and explainability, accountability, human-centricity
Fairness requires context-appropriate metrics, subgroup testing and documented trade-offs, because fairness metrics mathematically conflict
Safety and reliability means intended function under expected and unexpected conditions, with fail-safes and graceful failure
Privacy and security spans data minimization, de-identification, access control and AI-specific threat modelling
Transparency is about the organization disclosing AI use; explainability is about an individual output being understandable; interpretability is the underlying model property
Accountability is non-delegable: named humans answer for outcomes, and responsibility is who does the work
Human-centricity means AI augments human agency, which is operationalized through oversight, impact assessment and preserved choice

t_roles.overview: The cast of AI governance: board and executive leadership setting risk appetite, a cross-functional governance committee steering policy and reviews, and operating roles (privacy officers, CISOs, data scientists, legal counsel, ethics leads, business owners, frontline users) each holding a defined piece. Stakeholder mapping and RACI matrices keep interests and duties visible, and integration into enterprise risk management keeps AI risk from living in a silo.
t_roles.deep_dive:
### Three layers

| Layer | Roles | Owns |
|---|---|---|
| **Direction** | Board, CEO, COO, CRO, CISO, CDAO, CPO, CCO, CAIEO | Risk appetite, funding, tone, final accountability |
| **Steering** | AI governance board or council: legal, privacy, security, data science, ethics, risk, compliance, business units | Framework, high-risk use-case review, escalation decisions, upward reporting |
| **Operating** | Data scientists and AI engineers, data engineers, AI ops, product owners, risk officers, compliance, frontline users | Building, assessing, monitoring, documenting, flagging anomalies |

A growing number of organizations add a **Chief AI Ethics Officer** to hold the ethical governance remit explicitly, which is a signal of maturity rather than a legal requirement.

### RACI keeps it honest

RACI (Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed) is the instrument the BOK's "define roles and responsibilities" indicator points at. Applied per governance task rather than per department, it forces two things that org charts hide: exactly one accountable owner per task, and an explicit list of who must be consulted before the decision. Governance failures usually trace to a task with no accountable owner, or to a decision made without the function that would have caught the problem.

### Stakeholder mapping is a control

Stakeholder mapping identifies everyone affected by or influencing a system, internal and external: the business sponsor, the affected employees, the customers scored, the communities implicated, the vendors in the chain, the regulators with jurisdiction. Mapping them is not documentation for its own sake. A stakeholder who is never identified is a risk nobody owns, and external stakeholders (civil society, affected communities) are the ones internal processes most reliably miss.

### Integration into enterprise risk management

AI risk that lives in a separate register gets reviewed separately and funded last. The mature pattern is to tag AI risks inside the existing ERM portfolio, with AI-specific fields (system, model version, affected population, fairness exposure) rather than a parallel process. That is also how AI governance gets a board audience: it arrives through the risk reporting that already has one.
t_roles.exam:
Scenario questions test committee composition (multidisciplinary beats any single function), escalation paths, and stakeholder analysis. If an answer concentrates AI governance in one department (legal, IT, anyone), it is almost always wrong; the same is true of an answer that assigns a governance task without naming an accountable owner.

A second reliable angle: a scenario where a stakeholder group was overlooked (contract data labelers, the affected community, frontline staff who will actually operate the system) and the question asks what went wrong. The answer names the missing perspective, not the missing control.
key_points: Boards and executives own oversight and risk appetite; committees operationalize the framework; operating roles execute
Effective governance committees are multidisciplinary by design: legal, privacy, security, data science, ethics, risk, business
RACI matrices make each governance task's Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed roles explicit, with exactly one accountable owner
Stakeholder mapping covers everyone affected by or influencing a system, internal and external; unmapped stakeholders are unowned risks
AI risks should be tagged inside the existing enterprise risk management portfolio rather than kept in a parallel register
The Chief AI Ethics Officer role signals that ethical governance has an explicit owner
Cross-functional collaboration is a control in itself: siloed AI decisions are how governance failures start

t_training.overview: The workforce layer of governance: building AI literacy across the organization and role-specific competence where it counts, with executives who can weigh AI risk, developers who know governance by design, users trained for appropriate reliance, and governance staff current on law and standards. Since 2 February 2025 the EU AI Act has made AI literacy an explicit expectation for provider and deployer staff, which turns training from a culture initiative into a compliance obligation.
t_training.deep_dive:
The BOK's indicator is to "create and deliver a training and awareness program to all stakeholders on AI terminology, strategy and governance." Three design consequences follow.

### Awareness for everyone, depth by role

| Audience | What they need |
|---|---|
| **Executives and board** | Strategic alignment, regulatory exposure, reputational and enterprise risk, how to read an AI risk register |
| **Developers and data scientists** | Governance by design, documentation standards, bias and fairness testing, reproducibility, the approval workflow |
| **Legal, risk and compliance** | Regulatory fluency, impact assessment practice, vendor and contract risk, audit readiness |
| **Product and business owners** | Use-case vetting, success criteria, user impact, their accountability for outcomes |
| **Frontline users** | What the system can and cannot do, when to override, how to report an anomaly, recourse options |
| **IT and security** | Monitoring, incident response, control ownership, AI-specific attack surface |
| **Everyone** | Basic literacy, the organization's principles, how to escalate a concern |

### Training is a control against automation bias

Automation bias is the documented human tendency to over-trust machine output, and it is the reason oversight that exists on paper still fails. Training is the cheapest countermeasure: users who understand error modes, confidence and the system's limits are materially better overseers. Interface design carries the other half, by making disagreement and override easy.

### Maintenance is part of the obligation

A curriculum written before the current obligations existed does not satisfy them. Programs need a refresh cycle tied to regulatory change, and effectiveness measures rather than attendance counts: pre and post literacy assessment, the share of staff trained within a stated window, the number of AI projects with complete documentation, and the volume of risk escalations initiated by trained staff. The last one is the interesting metric, because it measures whether people believe reporting is safe.

### Change management is the unglamorous half

Workforce readiness is not only knowledge. New AI systems change workflows, job content and required skills, and the organizations that handle this badly generate the resistance that later shows up as shadow AI: employees using unapproved tools because the approved path is too slow. Readiness work is therefore also governance work.
t_training.exam:
Look for the role-tailoring principle: one-size-fits-all training is the wrong answer, and awareness for everyone plus depth by role is the right one. A scenario about over-reliance or automation bias usually resolves to user training plus interface safeguards, not to model retraining.

The date to know is 2 February 2025, when the EU AI Act's Article 4 AI literacy expectation took effect alongside the prohibitions. Questions sometimes test that second, less famous half of the date. And if an option treats training as a one-time onboarding event, it contradicts the maintenance requirement.
key_points: EU AI Act Article 4 makes AI literacy an expectation for provider and deployer staff from 2 February 2025, so training is compliance as well as culture
Tailor by role: executives (risk and strategy), developers (responsible build practices), users (capabilities, limits, appropriate reliance), governance staff (law and standards)
Training is a primary countermeasure to automation bias, the human tendency to over-trust machine output
Programs need refresh cycles tied to regulatory and system change; a stale curriculum does not satisfy a current obligation
Measure effectiveness with pre and post literacy assessment, completion rates, documentation completeness and escalations initiated by staff
Workforce readiness includes change management: new systems change workflows, job content and skills, and mishandled change produces shadow AI

t_devdeploy.overview: The value-chain role model that allocates governance duties: developers build and train models, curate data and test for fairness; deployers operationalize systems, monitor real-world behaviour and manage user-facing risk; users operate within intended bounds and report anomalies. BOK v2.1 adds providers to this list, and the BOK states that developer and deployer are task labels rather than legal categories. The EU AI Act formalizes a partly different cast (provider, deployer, importer, distributor) with obligations attached to each.
t_devdeploy.deep_dive:
### The BOK's roles, as tasks

| Role | Focus | Governance responsibilities |
|---|---|---|
| **Developer** | Data scientists, ML engineers, data engineers, research scientists | Data curation and rights, model selection and training, fairness and robustness evaluation, documentation, testing |
| **Provider** (added in v2.1) | The entity that places the system on the market under its own name, including a team that fine-tunes someone else's base model | Conformity, technical documentation, post-market monitoring, incident reporting for high-risk systems |
| **Deployer** | Software engineers, AI ops, product managers, infrastructure | Fit-for-context assessment, integration, human oversight in operation, monitoring, incident escalation, user instructions |
| **User** | Internal staff, external customers, decision-makers relying on output | Operate within intended bounds, apply judgment, report anomalies, exercise recourse |

The BOK's introduction says explicitly that "developer" and "deployer" are used as **task labels, not legal categories**. That is a deliberate signal: the same organization can be a developer for one system and a deployer for another, and the labels describe what you are doing rather than what you legally are.

### The EU AI Act's cast, as legal categories

| Role | Definition in outline | Core duties |
|---|---|---|
| **Provider** | Develops an AI system (or has it developed) and places it on the EU market or puts it into service under its own name or trademark | Risk management, data governance, technical documentation, conformity assessment, CE marking, registration, post-market monitoring, incident reporting |
| **Deployer** | Uses an AI system under its authority in a professional capacity | Use per instructions, assign competent human oversight, ensure input data relevance, monitor, retain logs, report serious incidents, and for some, run a fundamental rights impact assessment |
| **Importer** | Places a third-country provider's system on the EU market | Verify the conformity assessment was performed, documentation exists and CE marking is affixed |
| **Distributor** | Makes a system available on the EU market without modifying it | Verify CE marking and documentation, and do not supply systems it believes non-compliant |

### The role-shift trap

Under the EU AI Act, a deployer that puts its name or trademark on a high-risk system, substantially modifies it, or changes its intended purpose becomes the **provider** and inherits the provider's obligations. That single rule generates a disproportionate share of exam items, because it converts what looks like a deployment question into a conformity question.

### Why the split matters

Most of the risk everyone downstream inherits was determined upstream: training data, architecture, thresholds. But most of the harm happens downstream, in context, where the deployer chooses how the output is used and who oversees it. The role model exists so that neither party can point at the other, and so the exam can ask you who owes what.
t_devdeploy.exam:
Questions give you an entity and ask its obligations, or an obligation and ask whose it is. Watch the seam: an entity that rebrands or substantially modifies a high-risk system becomes the provider, and an option that assigns provider duties (conformity assessment, CE marking) to a deployer is wrong.

Keep the two vocabularies straight, because the exam mixes them. The BOK's developer / provider / deployer / user are task labels; the EU AI Act's provider / deployer / importer / distributor are legal categories with defined duties. A question that mentions CE marking or Annex IV documentation is asking about the legal cast; one about bias testing or data curation is asking about the task cast.

t_oversight.overview: How humans stay in charge of automated decisions: human-in-the-loop (a person approves each consequential decision), human-on-the-loop (a person supervises operation and can intervene), and human-in-command (humans set the bounds and can override or shut the system down). The right level is a risk decision, and GDPR Article 22 plus the EU AI Act's human-oversight requirement make it a legal one for high-stakes uses.
t_oversight.deep_dive:
### The three levels

| Level | What the human does | Suits |
|---|---|---|
| **Human-in-the-loop** | Reviews and approves each consequential decision before it takes effect | High-stakes, lower-volume decisions: medical triage, loan denial, custody or benefits determinations |
| **Human-on-the-loop** | Supervises operation, monitors outputs, can intervene or halt | Higher-volume, moderate-risk operation where per-decision review is impractical |
| **Human-in-command** | Sets objectives, bounds and escalation rules, and retains the ability to override or deactivate | Overall program governance, and the fallback for every deployed system |

### The legal hooks

**GDPR Article 22** gives individuals the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing that produces legal effects or similarly significantly affects them. The exceptions (contract necessity, law, explicit consent) come with mandatory safeguards: at minimum human intervention, the ability to express a view, and the ability to contest the decision. "Solely automated" is the hinge, which is why meaningful human review before the decision takes effect moves a process outside Article 22, and why cosmetic review does not.

**EU AI Act Article 14** requires high-risk systems to be designed so that competent humans can effectively oversee them, including the ability to understand the system's outputs, to disregard or override them, and to interrupt the system through a stop button or similar procedure. It also obliges deployers to assign oversight to people with the necessary competence, training and authority.

### What makes oversight real

The exam-relevant insight is that oversight is a design problem, not a staffing problem. A human who rubber-stamps every recommendation satisfies no obligation. Effective oversight needs four things at once:

- **Competence**: the overseer understands the system's limits and failure modes.
- **Information**: the interface presents what is needed to judge, including confidence and reasons, not just the recommendation.
- **Authority**: the overseer can actually reverse the output without career cost.
- **Time and volume**: the review load is small enough to permit real attention.

Take any one away and you have **automation bias with a witness**: a human who provides legal cover for a decision the machine already made. That is the failure the frameworks are written against, and it is why Article 22 speaks of human intervention rather than human presence.
t_oversight.exam:
A classic testable distinction: in-the-loop versus on-the-loop, plus scenarios asking which level a use case demands. The rule of thumb is risk and volume together: a high-stakes, low-volume decision supports per-decision review, while high-volume moderate-risk operation supports supervisory oversight with intervention.

The deeper point exam items reach for is that oversight must be meaningful. An option that satisfies an oversight obligation by adding a human who always accepts the model's output is wrong, as is one that treats oversight as a one-time approval rather than a continuing capability. If the stem mentions an interface that shows only the recommendation, the missing element is information.
key_points: Human-in-the-loop: per-decision human approval, suited to high-stakes, lower-volume decisions
Human-on-the-loop: supervisory monitoring with intervention power, suited to higher-volume moderate-risk operation
Human-in-command: humans set bounds and retain override and deactivation authority over the system

t_policy.overview: Retrofitting privacy and security policies for AI. Legacy policies assume data sits in databases with defined purposes, but AI repurposes data, retains it inside model weights, infers what was never collected, and exposes new attack surfaces (model inversion, membership inference, prompt injection, data poisoning). Acceptable-use, retention, access and incident policies all need AI-aware updates, and a data classification policy plus a data inventory are prerequisites.
t_policy.deep_dive:
### Where legacy policy breaks

| Policy area | The assumption AI breaks | The gap to close |
|---|---|---|
| **Purpose limitation** | Data collected for one purpose stays there | A compatibility analysis or new lawful basis before training on repurposed data; a use-case registry tagging each dataset with approved purposes |
| **Retention** | Deleting the record deletes the data | Retention rules covering derived data, checkpoints, embeddings, caches and the trained model itself, plus a stated position on what a deletion request means for a model |
| **Minimization** | Minimization applies to storage | Minimization applied to features and training sets; if fewer features perform equivalently, use fewer |
| **De-identification** | Removing names anonymizes | A standard that survives quasi-identifier combinations and model-based re-identification, with re-anonymization required when datasets are combined |
| **Access control** | Access is to databases | Access control over prompts, model endpoints, training environments, feature stores and model registries |
| **Incident response** | Incidents mean a breached database | Playbooks for model inversion, membership inference, prompt injection, poisoned training data and unintended memorization |

### The AI-specific threat list

- **Model inversion**: reconstructing training inputs by probing the model's outputs.
- **Membership inference**: determining whether a specific person's record was in the training set, which is itself a disclosure about that person.
- **Data poisoning**: corrupting training data to shape model behaviour.
- **Prompt injection**: crafting input that overrides an LLM's instructions or safety filters, including indirectly through retrieved content.
- **Unintended memorization**: a model reproducing fragments of sensitive training data on request.
- **Function creep**: expanding data use beyond the stated purpose through gradual AI reuse.

### Shadow AI and acceptable use

The most common real-world AI policy failure is not a sophisticated attack; it is an employee pasting customer data into an unapproved tool. Acceptable-use policy has to say what data may enter a prompt, which tools are approved, and what happens when someone needs something that is not on the list. Banning without providing an approved path reliably produces shadow AI, which is worse than the exposure it was meant to prevent.

### Prerequisites

Two things must exist before AI-specific policy can work: a **data classification policy** (so you know what is sensitive) and a **data inventory** (so you know where it is). The BOK states this directly. Without them, monitoring and managing AI training data is severely disadvantaged, and no amount of policy language compensates.
t_policy.exam:
Gap-analysis scenarios: a company adopts AI under legacy policies, and the question asks what breaks first. Strong answers name a concrete gap, such as retention schedules that never contemplated model weights, an incident response plan with no prompt-injection playbook, or the absence of a data inventory, rather than saying "update the policies."

Two other recurring angles. First, deletion requests against models: the tested insight is that a model retains data in learned form, so deletion has to address the model, not only the database, and the honest answer may be retraining. Second, security: model inversion and membership inference are offered as exotic options and are the correct answers more often than people expect, because they are precisely what conventional threat models omit.

t_thirdparty.overview: Vendor risk, AI edition. Organizations increasingly buy AI capability (pretrained models, APIs, labeling services, cloud platforms), importing risks that traditional third-party risk management never probed: opaque training data, sub-tier suppliers, silently changing model versions, and contractual gaps around fairness, audit and incidents. The BOK covers this under policies, assessments and contracts, across procurement, supply chain, human resources and acceptable use.
t_thirdparty.deep_dive:
### Why AI slips past conventional TPRM

| Conventional TPRM checks | What it misses about AI |
|---|---|
| Financial solvency, insurance, certification | Training data of unknown origin or rights status |
| Standard security questionnaires | Model behaviour that changes with each vendor update |
| Contract templates for services | Liability allocation for harmful or discriminatory output |
| Named-subcontractor disclosure | Sub-tier data labelers, base-model suppliers and open-source dependencies |

The structural problem is that a vendor's model is a black box inside a black box: you cannot inspect the training data, you often cannot see the model version, and you may not learn that behaviour changed until your users report it. Point-in-time diligence therefore decays fast.

### Four-part response

**1. Flag AI at procurement intake.** Modify intake to ask whether the product includes AI, ML, LLMs or automated decision-making; whether your data will train their models; and whether personal, biometric or sensitive data is processed. Flagged deals get supplemental review by legal, risk and technical stakeholders. Not all vendors volunteer their AI use, so the question must be asked rather than inferred.

**2. Run AI-specific due diligence.** Training-data origin and rights; fairness and robustness test evidence; explainability support; model-change practices; security of the ML supply chain; and named sub-tier dependencies (who labeled the data, whose base model is underneath). A standardized supplier questionnaire mapped to risk tiers keeps this repeatable.

**3. Write the contract terms that make risk manageable.**

| Clause | What it should secure |
|---|---|
| Data-use limits | No customer data used for retraining without explicit consent |
| Fairness and performance | Warranties, plus evidence of testing and remediation of disparate impact |
| Model-change notification | Advance notice of updates that change behaviour or intended use |
| Incident notification | Time-bound reporting (for example within 24 hours) and defined responsibilities |
| Audit rights | The right to audit or inspect high-risk vendor systems, and to receive documentation |
| Termination and portability | Exit conditions, model deactivation rights, and data return or deletion |

**4. Monitor continuously.** Continuous monitoring beats point-in-time diligence because vendor model updates change behaviour mid-contract. An **AI system bill of materials** listing upstream inputs is the emerging instrument for visibility into the sub-tier chain, and open-source components need the same licensing, vulnerability and bias review as commercial ones.

### The line that does not move

Accountability is non-delegable. Outsourcing the AI does not outsource the regulatory or ethical responsibility, and the EU AI Act reinforces this by attaching obligations to whoever places a system on the market or uses it, not to whoever built it furthest upstream.
t_thirdparty.exam:
Scenarios ask what due diligence or contract terms an AI procurement demands. Strong answers are AI-specific: training-data provenance, bias testing evidence, model-change notification, audit rights, incident SLAs. Answers that list only generic vendor checks (financials, insurance, SOC 2) are engineered to be incomplete.

The other reliable angle is the sub-tier question: a vendor that subcontracts data labeling, fine-tunes someone else's base model, or ships open-source dependencies has extended your exposure past your contractual counterparty. And a question that frames outsourcing as transferring responsibility is wrong: accountability stays with the deploying organization.

term:AI Agent.deep_dive:
The defining loop is **perceive, decide, act**: an agent senses its environment and autonomously takes actions toward goals, rather than only returning a prediction when asked. The distinction from a plain model is not sophistication but agency: a model produces output, an agent changes state in the world (sending mail, moving money, calling APIs, editing files).

That shift is why agentic AI dominates current governance discussion. Governance controls that were adequate for a model in a human workflow become insufficient when the system has its own tool access, because actions execute without a human between inference and effect. The controls that follow are the ones you would design for any autonomous actor: a defined and least-privilege **action space**, human approval checkpoints for consequential or irreversible steps, logging of every action taken, spending and rate limits, and a kill switch that actually stops the agent rather than just the interface.

BOK v2.1 reflects this in Domain IV.A, which now names **agentic architectures** alongside fine-tuning and retrieval-augmented generation as a deployment option a governance professional must evaluate. Agentic systems also widen the prompt-injection surface, because an agent that reads untrusted content and holds tool credentials can be instructed by that content.
term:AI Agent.exam_tip: The words 'takes action' in a scenario are the tell: a system that acts on its environment is an agent, not just a model. When a stem describes an agent, the expected control is almost always a limit on its action space, a human approval checkpoint, or logging, not a model retraining.

term:AI System.deep_dive:
This is the legally loaded definition, and it decides whether a regulation applies at all. The EU AI Act (Article 3(1)) and the OECD's 2023 revision both define an AI system as a **machine-based system** that, for **explicit or implicit objectives**, **infers** from the input it receives how to generate outputs such as **predictions, content, recommendations or decisions** that can **influence physical or virtual environments**.

Four elements carry the weight:

- **Machine-based**: it runs on hardware, which excludes pure human decision processes.
- **Explicit or implicit objectives**: the goal need not be coded; a learned objective counts.
- **Infers**: the operative word. The system derives outputs rather than executing a rule that was written down for each case. This is what separates AI from ordinary rule-following software.
- **Influence on environments**: the output has to be able to affect something, physically or virtually, which is broad enough to cover a recommendation a human then acts on.

ISO/IEC 22989 adds the structural vocabulary around it: an AI system is composed of **AI components** (models, data pipelines, inference engines, knowledge bases), which is why risk analysis decomposes a system into parts even though governance attaches to the assembled whole.
term:AI System.exam_tip: Recite the elements: machine-based, explicit or implicit objectives, infers from input, generates predictions/content/recommendations/decisions, can influence environments. Whether something is an AI system is a threshold question: if it fails this definition, the EU AI Act does not apply to it at all.

term:Artificial General Intelligence (AG.deep_dive:
AGI is hypothetical AI with **human-level competence across essentially all cognitive domains**, able to transfer learning between unrelated tasks the way a person does. It does not exist. Every deployed system today, however broad, is narrow AI, because generality is about transfer across unrelated domains rather than the size of the training set.

The distinction does real work in governance. It disciplines risk assessment, because claims about a system's capabilities should be bounded by what has been demonstrated rather than what is conceivable. It disciplines marketing, because describing a product as general or near-general intelligence invites consumer-protection exposure. And it disciplines long-term risk debate, which is about systems that do not yet exist and therefore cannot be regulated by capability benchmarks.

For a governance professional the practical rule is: treat AGI as a taxonomic boundary, not a planning input. When a scenario asks you to reason about a real system, the correct framing is always the narrow, bounded one.
term:Artificial General Intelligence (AG.exam_tip: ISO/IEC 22989 calls this general AI (broad range of tasks at a satisfactory level). Expand 'GAI' from context: a capability-ladder stem means general AI (theoretical); a NIST AI 600-1 stem means generative AI. Any option treating a current product, however broad, as AGI is wrong.

term:Artificial Superintelligence (ASI).deep_dive:
ASI is the hypothetical tier beyond AGI: intelligence surpassing the best human performance in essentially every domain. It has no engineering path, no deployed instance, and no agreed definition beyond "better than us at everything."

Its role in a governance syllabus is taxonomic and rhetorical. Taxonomically, it is the far end of the capability ladder, and knowing where the ladder ends is how you avoid misclassifying real systems. Rhetorically, it appears in long-term-risk argument, in frontier-lab safety framing, and occasionally in vendor marketing, where it should be read as a claim requiring substantiation rather than a description.

Practically, the governance instruments you would use for an ASI do not exist, which is why serious long-term-risk work focuses on the precursor capabilities and on the institutional capacity to notice and respond. For exam purposes, ASI is a placement question.
term:Artificial Superintelligence (ASI).exam_tip: Ladder recall: narrow (exists), AGI (theoretical), ASI (theoretical). Placement questions here are free points, and any option implying a deployed ASI is wrong.

term:Complexity.deep_dive:
Complexity is the characteristic of AI systems that defeats intuition and simple review: many interacting components, high-dimensional models, and behaviour that emerges from the interactions rather than from any single part.

It is a risk source in its own right. ISO/IEC 23894's Annex B catalogs AI risk sources, and system complexity and lifecycle complexity both appear there, because more moving parts mean more failure modes, harder root-cause analysis, and more places for a control to be assumed but not present. In an AI system the complexity is layered: the model itself, the data pipeline that feeds it, the integration that calls it, the human workflow around it, and the third-party components inside all of those.

The governance response is not to demand simplicity, which would mean abandoning the capability. It is to decompose deliberately: document the components and their interfaces, test at the boundaries as well as end to end, and build the observability that makes a failure traceable to a cause. Layered controls (testing, monitoring, oversight) exist precisely because no single control can see the whole system.
term:Complexity.exam_tip: Complexity justifies layered controls: testing plus monitoring plus oversight. An option concluding that a system is 'too complex to govern' or 'too complex to explain' is never the right answer; the right answer decomposes the system and adds controls.

term:Convolutional Neural Network (CNN).deep_dive:
The CNN is the neural architecture built for grid-like data. Convolutional filters slide across an image learning local patterns in layers (edges, then textures, then parts, then objects), sharing weights across positions so the network needs far fewer parameters than a dense network would for the same task.

It is the architecture behind computer vision: image classification, object detection, medical imaging, facial recognition. That lineage means CNNs inherit vision's governance flashpoints directly. A face-recognition CNN used to identify people is processing **biometric data for unique identification**, which is a special category under GDPR Article 9, and the same use case sits in both the EU AI Act's prohibited practices (untargeted facial-image scraping, real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces) and its Annex III high-risk categories.

There is also a security dimension: vision models are the classic target of adversarial examples, where small, often imperceptible perturbations flip a classification. NIST AI 100-2 catalogs this as evasion. For governance, the practical point is that a CNN's accuracy figure describes average behaviour, not behaviour under an input chosen to break it.
term:Convolutional Neural Network (CNN).exam_tip: Architecture matching: CNN for images and spatial data, RNN or LSTM for sequences, transformer for modern language. When a scenario involves cameras identifying people, move immediately to biometric and special-category analysis.

term:Deep Learning.deep_dive:
Deep learning is machine learning with many-layered neural networks that learn hierarchical representations directly from raw data, removing the hand-engineered features that earlier approaches required. It is what made modern vision, speech and language AI possible, and it is the paradigm that turned opacity into a governance problem: capability arrived at the cost of inspectability.

Two governance consequences follow from the mechanism. First, because representations are learned rather than specified, the system's behaviour is a property of its training data, so data governance becomes model governance. Second, because the learned weights carry no legible logic, explanation has to be reconstructed after the fact, which is why post-hoc explainability techniques (SHAP, LIME, counterfactuals) exist at all.

The subset relationships are worth keeping straight: deep learning is a subset of machine learning, which is a subset of AI. "Deep" refers to the number of layers in the network, not to the depth of the system's understanding.
term:Deep Learning.exam_tip: Deep learning is a subset of machine learning, which is a subset of AI, and 'deep' means many layers. Distractors often describe deep learning as a separate technology from ML rather than a family within it.

term:Expert System.deep_dive:
An expert system is classic symbolic AI in production form: a **knowledge base** of rules hand-encoded from human experts, plus an **inference engine** that applies them to facts. In narrow, well-bounded domains (medical diagnosis aids, equipment configuration, tax rules) they performed well, and they were transparent by construction, because the rules could be read and argued with.

Their limitation is brittleness at the edge of coded knowledge. Anything the experts did not encode, the system cannot handle, and rules that interact in unforeseen ways produce surprising conclusions. Machine learning displaced them because learning patterns from data generalises better than enumerating rules by hand.

They remain the standard contrast case in governance discussions, and a useful one. An expert system is explainable and auditable by inspection, which is why the design guidance in this space still says that for eligibility decisions a rule-based system may be more appropriate than a black-box model. The trade is capability against explainability, and the governance professional is the person who has to make that trade explicit rather than defaulting to the more capable option.
term:Expert System.exam_tip: Rule-based, explainable, brittle: expert systems are the contrast case to learned, opaque, generalising ML. Expect them as an answer option when a scenario needs an inherently interpretable decision method.

term:Feedforward Neural Network (FFNN).deep_dive:
The feedforward network is the baseline neural architecture: information flows in one direction, from input through hidden layers to output, with no cycles and no memory of previous inputs. Each layer applies weights and an activation function to the previous layer's output, and training adjusts those weights by backpropagation.

It is the building block the specialised architectures elaborate on. Add recurrence and you get memory across time steps (RNN, LSTM); add convolution and weight sharing over a grid and you get spatial pattern learning (CNN); add attention and you get the transformer that underpins modern language models. Knowing the baseline is what makes the specialisations legible.

Governance relevance is indirect but real: an FFNN is a learned, opaque function approximator, so it carries the same opacity problem as any deep model, and its capacity is set by architecture choices (depth, width) that a governance professional should see documented alongside the training data and evaluation results.
term:Feedforward Neural Network (FFNN).exam_tip: Architecture taxonomy anchor: feedforward means no memory, recurrent means sequence memory, convolutional means spatial patterns, transformer means attention. Four one-line pairings cover most architecture-recognition items.

term:Foundation Model.deep_dive:
A foundation model is pretrained once on broad, varied data and then adapted to many downstream uses by fine-tuning, prompting or retrieval. The term was popularised by Stanford researchers (Bommasani et al., 2021) to capture the shift from task-specific models to a general base that many applications sit on.

Its breadth is the governance problem. Defects and biases in the base model are inherited by every application built on it, and the organizations adapting it typically have little or no visibility into its training data, its data rights, or how it was evaluated. That inheritance is why NIST AI 600-1 names **value-chain and component integration** as a generative-AI risk, and why the controls that matter are the ones that travel with the model: model cards, documentation of training data, stated limitations, and downstream information.

The EU AI Act regulates the same idea under a different label, **general-purpose AI model** (Article 3(63)). Worth knowing precisely: the final Act text does not use the phrase foundation model at all, so an exam stem saying 'foundation model' is describing the EU's GPAI concept.
term:Foundation Model.exam_tip: When a stem says foundation model, think of the EU's general-purpose AI model: one broadly capable base model adapted downstream into many applications, with the provider owing documentation, downstream information, a copyright policy and a training-content summary.

term:Generative AI.deep_dive:
Generative AI creates new content (text, images, audio, video, code) by learning the distribution of its training data and sampling from it. Large language models and diffusion models are the exemplars. The mechanism is what produces the risk profile: because output is generated rather than retrieved, plausibility and truth are separate properties.

NIST's Generative AI Profile names twelve risks unique to or amplified by GAI. The ones that recur on the exam: **confabulation** (confidently stated false content), **harmful bias and homogenization**, **information integrity** (deepfakes, disinformation, eroded trust in authentic media), **data privacy** (training-data leakage and memorization), **information security**, **intellectual property**, and **value-chain integration** risk. Alongside them sit four cross-cutting considerations: governance, content provenance, pre-deployment testing, and incident disclosure.

Generative is not the same as general. Generative describes what the system produces; general describes the breadth of its intelligence. Confusing the two is the most common misreading in this area.
term:Generative AI.exam_tip: Generative describes output (content), general describes capability (AGI). Expect the risk bundle to be tested: confabulation, memorization leakage, synthetic media, IP exposure, and the injection surface.
